latin.title: The Suburban Baths at Pompeii
latin.body: The Suburban Baths at Pompeii, built just outside the Marine Gate around 50 BCE, contained a surprise: an upstairs chamber decorated with explicit erotic frescoes in eight separate panels. Unlike the apotropaic phalluses found elsewhere in the city, these images depicted specific sexual acts in careful detail. Scholars debate whether this room served clients seeking prostitutes or simply displayed the sort of sophisticated eroticism common in wealthy Roman homes. The baths themselves followed standard design—frigidarium, tepidarium, caldarium—but this private space suggests activities conducted furtim, away from the public pools below. When Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE, it preserved not just the mechanical efficiency of Roman bathing culture but also evidence of desires pursued in shadows, the secret commerce that thrived in a port city's margins.

greek.title: Diogenes in the Marketplace
greek.body: Diogenes of Sinope made shamelessness a philosophy. Living in a clay jar in the Athenian agora during the 340s BCE, he urinated in public, ate in the marketplace, and mocked passersby. When Alexander the Great visited and asked what favor he desired, Diogenes told him to stop blocking the sunlight. He masturbated openly, declaring that if only hunger could be satisfied by rubbing one's belly. The Cynics, whose name derived from "dog-like," rejected conventional shame as mere social artifice. Where Plato's Republic condemned the shameless democrat, Diogenes transformed ἀναίδεια into virtue, arguing that social convention corrupted natural human freedom. He carried a lamp through Athens in daylight, claiming to search for an honest man. His contemporary critics found him repulsive; later Stoics honored him as a sage who lived according to nature rather than custom.

french.title: Rimbaud's Season in London and Brussels
french.body: In 1873, Arthur Rimbaud and Paul Verlaine fled Paris for London, then Brussels, their partnership combusting in alcohol and violence. Rimbaud was nineteen, already abandoning verse for prose poems that would become "Les Illuminations." The manuscript circulated in fragments for years before Verlaine published it in 1886, three years after Rimbaud had vanished into Africa as a coffee trader. In these pieces, Rimbaud dismantled poetic tradition with hallucinatory images of urban spectacle: fairgrounds, electric lights, phantom crowds. He called it "alchemy of the word," a deliberate derangement of the senses. The fanfares and parades in his visions summoned not celebration but estrangement, the mechanical repetition of modern entertainments. By twenty-one, Rimbaud had renounced literature entirely. He never wrote another line, spending his final years trading guns in Abyssinia, silent about the poems that would remake French poetry.

german.title: Schopenhauer's Frankfurt Routine
german.body: Arthur Schopenhauer kept a rigid daily schedule in his Frankfurt lodgings from 1833 until his death in 1860. He woke at seven, wrote until noon without interruption, then played the flute for exactly one hour. After a solitary lunch at the Englischer Hof, he walked for two hours with his succession of poodles, each named Atma (Sanskrit for world-soul). He read The Times in the reading room, then returned home for evening study. This mechanical routine served a philosophical purpose: by reducing life to predictable rhythms, he believed he could minimize the Will's torments and achieve the contemplative detachment his philosophy prescribed. His neighbors considered him eccentric and quarrelsome. He once shoved a seamstress down his stairs for disturbing his morning work, leading to a lawsuit that cost him a quarterly pension for twenty years.

oldenglish.title: The Battle of Brunanburh, 937
oldenglish.body: In 937, King Athelstan faced a coalition of Norse Dublin, Scottish, and Strathclyde forces at an unidentified site scholars call Brunanburh. The battle proved decisive: five kings and seven jarls fell, along with Constantine II's son. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle commemorates the victory in 73 lines of alliterative verse, composed within living memory of the event. The poet surveys the corpse-strewn field where carrion birds gather, calling it the greatest slaughter on British soil since the Angles and Saxons first crossed the North Sea. This poem, copied into four manuscript versions of the Chronicle, stands apart from the usual terse annals. Its language echoes Beowulf and Genesis, suggesting a court poet shaped the victory into heroic verse while participants still lived to remember.
